title: Role of chirality in the polarizer-filter dichotomy in nonmagnetic junctions
abstract: Chirality-induced spin selectivity can enable spin generation by nonmagnetic junctions, but its symmetry requirements remain debated. We show that the symmetry of the junction constrains its polarizing behavior: a spin polarizer requires a chiral junction, whereas an achiral junction can act as a spin filter. This symmetry involves the junction as a whole, not only the molecule. Achiral molecules can act as polarizers or filters depending on junction geometry, as confirmed with a minimal tight-binding model. Reciprocity forbids polarization detection by linear two-terminal magnetoresistance; we propose a nonlocal measurement that distinguishes polarizers from filters and establishes whether the junction breaks time-reversal symmetry.
summary: This work establishes that the symmetry of a nonmagnetic junction, rather than just the molecule's chirality, determines if it functions as a spin polarizer or a spin filter. By analyzing scattering matrices and proposing a nonlocal measurement technique, the authors provide a theoretical framework to distinguish these two distinct spin-filtering behaviors in mesoscopic junctions.
main_problem: The paper investigates the fundamental relationship between the symmetry of a nonmagnetic junction and its ability to act as a spin polarizer versus a spin filter.
main_result: The junction's symmetry dictates its behavior: a polarizer requires a chiral junction symmetry, while a filter is associated with an improper lead-exchanging symmetry. A nonlocal measurement is proposed to experimentally distinguish between these two classes.
method: The analysis uses scattering matrices ($S$) derived from a minimal tight-binding model, applying symmetry operations ($g$) to constrain the transmission and reflection probabilities ($P_t, P_r$).
model_or_system: The system is a nonmagnetic junction connecting leads (L and R) to a central structure, modeled as a four-atom chain whose symmetry is controlled by the dihedral angle ($\omega$).
key_observables: Polarization probabilities ($P_t, P_r$), nonlocal magnetoresistance signals ($\Delta V_{L,R}$), and spin accumulation ($m_{L,R}$).
important_parameters: The dihedral angle ($\omega$), which controls the junction's symmetry (e.g., $C_2$ vs. achiral).
main_assumptions: The analysis assumes elastic transport and relies on symmetry constraints derived from the lead-exchanging operation ($g$).
figures_summary: Figure 2 shows $P_t$ and $P_r$ vs. energy for different angles, classifying configurations as polarizers or filters. Figure 3 illustrates the nonlocal detection signals and resulting spin accumulations for both polarizer and filter cases.
paper_structure: The paper establishes the theoretical framework using scattering matrices and symmetry constraints (Table I), applies this to a minimal tight-binding model (Figure 2), and finally proposes and analyzes a nonlocal measurement technique using ferromagnetic probes to experimentally distinguish between polarizers and filters (Figure 3).
why_interesting: It provides a rigorous symmetry-based classification scheme for spin-dependent transport in nonmagnetic junctions, which is crucial for designing spintronic devices without relying on intrinsic magnetic order.

(a) A twisted chain with a C2 axis normal to the page forms a chiral junction polarizing transmitted and re- flected electrons (purple arrows) in the same direction: it is a polarizer. (b) A tilted planar chain with an inversion cen- ter (×) forms an achiral junction polarizing transmitted and reflected electrons oppositely: it is a filter. Larger atoms are closer to the viewer.

Transmitted polarization Pt (solid) and reflected po- larization Pr (dashed) vs energy E for a four-atom chain be- tween leads oriented along ˆz (blue: source, red: drain), for configurations with different dihedral angles ω, schematically shown on the left. (a),(b) Polarizers: chiral junctions with a lead-exchanging C2 axis, ω = 65◦(a) and ω = 0 tilted about the C2 axis (b). (c) Filter: achiral junction with an inversion center, ω = 180◦, tilted so that the molecular plane does not contain ˆz. (d) Junction without symmetry, ω = 65◦with a generic tilt: polarizer or filter depending on E. Larger atoms are closer to the viewer.
